$description: A source-neutral reference for the friendly, plain-spoken register most consumer and SMB SaaS products aim for. Original prose synthesized from public plain-language standards (plainlanguage.gov, GOV.UK) and permissively documented content systems — not tied to any single company's style guide.

voice.identity: A knowledgeable colleague talking a busy person through their own work — direct, warm, and specific. The product speaks like one competent human, not like a brand campaign and not like a terms-of-service document.

attributes.name: Direct
attributes.description: Say the thing. Lead with the point, keep sentences short, and cut every word that exists only to sound professional.

attributes.name: Warm without performing
attributes.description: Friendliness comes from being helpful and unhurried, not from exclamation marks. One genuine sentence beats three enthusiastic ones.

attributes.name: Concrete
attributes.description: Name the object, the amount, the date, the next step. Vague copy reads as either evasive or unfinished.

attributes.name: Respectful of attention
attributes.description: Assume the reader is mid-task. Front-load meaning, keep lines scannable, and never make someone read a paragraph to find the button.

attributes.name: Calm under failure
attributes.description: When something breaks, the voice gets quieter, not cuter. State what happened and the next move; playfulness disappears entirely.

tone_shifts.onboarding: Encouraging and momentum-building. Get the person to a first concrete win quickly; skip the tour of everything the product can theoretically do.
tone_shifts.success: Brief and genuine. Confirm what just happened in plain words, then get out of the way — or point at one sensible next step.
tone_shifts.errors: Plain, steady, useful. What happened, why if knowing helps, what to do now. No jokes, no blame, no apology theatre.
tone_shifts.billing-and-legal: Slightly more formal and completely unambiguous. Amounts, dates, and currencies must be exact on first read. Humor never appears here.
tone_shifts.empty-states: Instructive and forward-looking. Say what this view is for, what will appear once there's activity, and offer one clear action.

avoid: delight (as a verb aimed at the user)
simply / just (minimizers that read as condescension when the task isn't simple)
never: Internal codenames or schema names in user-facing copy
Slang that will read as dated within a year
Idioms or references that assume one country's cultural context

grammar.voice: Active voice, named actor. 'We emailed your receipt' — not 'A receipt has been emailed.'
grammar.contractions: Use them. It's, you're, we'll — they make copy sound like a person. Skip them only in legal text where precision outranks warmth.
grammar.person: Address the reader as 'you'; the product or company is 'we'. Never 'the user' in anything the user reads.
grammar.titles: Sentence case for buttons, headings, and page titles. Reserve capitals for proper nouns and product names.
grammar.numbers: Spell out one through nine in prose; numerals for 10 and up. Money, percentages, measurements, and times are always numerals.
grammar.abbreviations: Expand on first use, abbreviate after. No periods inside acronyms.
grammar.dates-and-times: Spell out the month and include the time zone — 'March 4, 2026 at 2:00 pm ET'. All-numeric dates mean different things in different countries.

errors.structure: What happened, in the reader's terms → what to do next. Cause only when it changes what they'd do. Never blame, never expose internals.
errors.example-good: We couldn't save your changes — your session expired. Sign in again and your draft will still be here.

empty-states.structure: Name what this view is → what will fill it → one clear action.
empty-states.example-good: Nothing exported yet. Reports you export will be listed here. Export your first report.

success.structure: Confirm the specific thing that happened → one next step, only if a natural one exists.
success.example-good: Your report is scheduled for Monday at 9:00 am ET. We'll email you when it's ready.

rules: Use 'they/them' when a person's gender is unknown.
Describe actions, not assumed abilities — 'works with screen readers' rather than ability-based shorthand.
Replace disability metaphors with the plain idea: 'gap' for 'blind spot', 'out of touch' for 'tone-deaf'.
Skip idioms that assume one country's context; translate the idea instead.
Make no assumptions about family structure, employment type, or physical ability.
